replies.author: PimpinPumpkin
replies.text:
Hey guys, I'm the author of Vela. First of all, thank you for posting about it here, as the project is really getting some traction now.

Yes, the project is sometimes buggy, sometimes very much so. I've stabilized the development branches a bit more lately, and spent a good deal of time trying to polish the experience vs adding new features. I have a stable branch (the default), a nightly branch, and a canary branch (the most chaotic and bleeding edge).

As others have pointed out, AI is absolutely used in this project. I would not have the time to manually maintain a project of this complexity otherwise (I do have an acquaintance who helped out briefly in the very beginning, otherwise it was all me). There's translations, documentation, and the code itself. While I am a professional developer, this is my first foray into Android development. I've been a user of GrapheneOS and FOSS software for many years now, and I saw the influx of vibecoded slop hit every corner of the internet. I like to think you all here are more intelligent than the idiots on Reddit (I lurked some threads over there) who think that just because an LLM was involved means the project is A) unethical or B) just as bad as Google Maps.

Even if you think that Vela gives the same amount of data to Google (it doesn't, I've covered this on my repo), consider the fact that modern Google Maps just straight up does not work anymore without Google services. It used to, and that's how I survived. The fact of the matter is I made Vela to solve my own problems. I hope it's an assurance that I use Vela as my primary navigation app. Whenever I drive, I make note of the bugs I had and try to fix them.

Also, I am reopening my investigation into making this work with Android Auto. More discussion is on Github.

Thanks!

replies.author: PimpinPumpkin
replies.text:
becomeparmesan I'm reworking the way offline pieces work substantially. The canaries are the bleeding edge right now, but basically I am moving to the OBF format used by OsmAnd. I'm not using their actual OBFs though since OsmAnd is architected completely differently. It's just a good, space-saving format.

Additionally, the POIs that appear on the map when you're just flicking around are not actually coming from Google. They are loaded from Overture data hosted on my repo. Overture is an aggregate of Meta/Facebook business pages, Bing data, and more. I will likely add more sources of POIs and potentially spin that off into a separate project. Once we are all settled, you will be able to search POIs offline if you have a given area downloaded. When you actually tap on a restaurant for example, we do send a search out to Google to correlate that with the Overture POI so we can get business hours, reviews, and photos. This is toggleable in settings though.

For routing, you can use the share button to share a Google Maps link, map pin, coordinates, address, or just open the gmaps link in the browser.

replies.author: DeletedUser1181
replies.text:
basic-channel A fair concern. It's important to preface that security is a never ending pursuit. What matters most to me, even for transparently vibe coded applications, is that the author has configured server-side security checks for easy to spot bad code (under the .github folder), has a SECURITY.md for a formal vulnerability reporting policy (else, real vulns get lumped in with random bug reports and feature requests), and ideally would also report a software bill of materials to audit the licenses and dependency vulnerability scanning. In the former, you want to make sure the project isn't violating other's software licenses and the latter is useful in identifying supply chain vulnerabilities.

I'm not as familiar with phone apps as I am with SAST tools for the same for more traditional scientific computing languages, so others would need to comment. But a quick scan of the ci.yml doesn't strike me as running SAST and other insecure code sniffing tools server-side. Just scanning the comments of the file. They could be doing this locally but we can't really know.

The effort seems genuine here and the developer is a user here, I think these are simple enough additions they'd be willing to make.

I use it with Obtainium and add a 30 day delay on updates.

As of today the repo has: private vulnerability reporting switched on, with the policy in SECURITY.md; a security workflow that scans the source on every push and pull request; Dependabot alerts on the libraries the build actually resolves, with the bill of materials exportable from the repo's Insights page; every GitHub Action pinned to an exact commit; and an OpenSSF Scorecard run. On the app side, device backups no longer include the Google web session or location history, and the embedded web pages cannot read files. SECURITY.md lists all of it, including what is still open. Scanners miss things, so if you read the code and something looks wrong, report it there.

I am using Claude Opus and Fable for audits of Vela perodically (basically when I feel I've done enough work to warranty it) if that helps at all. Another thing to note is that by design Vela has no backend, so data exfiltration is less of a concern. Of course, being open source, I encourage you all to look at the code. I'm pretty new to Android development as I've mentioned in the past, so if you have suggestions I am all ears. Thank you to all who have contributed so far!

DeletedUser1181

Ok, I checked your two addresses against the data Vela ships for DC and I see what is going on. Two changes are built. An entry Overture itself is unsure about now needs a second source before it ranks that high. And the data build now removes places that Foursquare, OpenStreetMap or Wikidata list as closed. That took out a large portion of businesses that were closed for a while. Both reach the app as regions are rebuilt over the next week or so. I could not find a CIA Museum at 550 17th St in the current file; if it still shows for you after that, tell me the build number.

Additionally, I've started Vela Almanac, which will eventually be the new source for 'Vela data' (businesses and POI icons). I'm building scrapers for business licenses, liquor licenses, etc, and building on top of Overture/AllThePlaces/OSM to rank each place by likelyhood of it still being open. That's what every project I've seen thus far is missing; continuous updates. The data will be AGPLv3 for anyone to use as long as they give due credit, so other projects can make use of this. Not to jork my pumpkin stalk, but this is pretty cool stuff. For those that are not familiar with AllThePlaces, I'm basically borrowing their concept but hitting US institutional datasets in addition. Yes, this will be US only for now, and I am literally just starting work on this now, so bear with me.

becomeparmesan Vela Almanac will save our souls. It's pretty amazing the huge sponsors they have over there for having such garbage in their mix.

replies.text:
marq2 Yes, there is an open pinned issue on GH. Right now for us GrapheneOS users, using Gearslip is the best option for getting an Android Auto experience in the car with Vela. Vela actually inspired the project, and the dev and I have been talking, and there is a big update coming hopefully soon that will improve compatibility with newer cars.

But either way, I am all for poking for ways to make Vela on AA work for others. It already works with stock Android if you use KingInstaller.

I don't personally use AA, so if you want to submit code to make the AA experience more like Gmaps, more functional, prettier, etc, all would be appreciated.
